q: He who lives in harmony with himself lives in harmony with the universe

credit: Disputed — attributed to Marcus Aurelius, but no text of the Meditations has been found containing this sentence, and the passage it is routinely cited to — Book X, 6 — says something else. The closest genuine line is Meditations IV, 23: "Everything harmonizes with me, which is harmonious to thee, O Universe."

credit: Not Freud's own line. The modern "insult instead of a stone" wording is documented by Quote Investigator in Robert Byrne, 1,911 Best Things Anybody Ever Said (New York: Fawcett Columbine, 1988). Attribution to Freud as author: unsupported.

real: An unnamed "former college president" — quoted by Dwight D. Eisenhower
credit: Dwight D. Eisenhower did not say "What is important is seldom urgent and what is urgent is seldom important." Addressing the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches at Evanston, Illinois, on 19 August 1954, he quoted "the statement of a former college president": "I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent." The word "seldom" does not appear in the speech, and Eisenhower did not claim the line as his own. Quote Investigator traces the hedged wording to listeners' retellings beginning later in 1954. — Quotle.info
cite: Dwight D. Eisenhower, "Address at the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches, Evanston, Illinois," 19 August 1954, The American Presidency Project, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/address-the-second-assembly-the-world-council-churches-evanston-illinois. The popular "seldom…seldom" wording does not appear in that address; for its transmission see Quote Investigator, "Quote Origin: What Is Important Is Seldom Urgent and What Is Urgent Is Seldom Important," 9 May 2014, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/09/urgent/.
